reports.title: GALLERY: College Heavy Hitters Presented by Columbia PFG gets rolling on Douglas Lake
reports.text:
JEFFERSON CO., Tenn. – The hunt began Sunday morning for the Douglas Lake bass that would crown the first-ever College Fishing Heavy Hitters Presented by Columbia PFG champions. Eighteen college teams took off from the Dandridge Boat Ramp to compete in the first-of-its-kind college-level “every fish counts” tournament with a $2,000 big-fish prize and the coveted heavyweight belts awaiting.
This event is hosted by Visit Jefferson County.

Competition at College Fishing Heavy Hitters will run from 8 a.m. to 3 p.m. CT. Follow the live-scoring action at SCORETRACKERLIVE.com and on MLF and Columbia PFG social media channels.

reports.title: Remembering Bill Taylor: “He was one of the greatest guys I knew”
reports.text:
A longtime FLW and MLF tournament director and the recipient of the Bass Fishing Hall of Fame’s Meritorious Service Award in 2025, Bill Taylor recently passed away after a short battle with liver cancer.
In the 1980’s, Taylor was a fierce competitor on the water. He fished the first Operation Bass tournament in 1980, and during his tournament career, racked up more than $500,000 in winnings and more than a dozen victories, including the 1981 Ranger Classic Championship and the 1984 Kentucky Bass Association State Championship.

reports.title: Bill Taylor: A life devoted to bass fishing and the people in it
reports.text:
Major League Fishing and the entire bass fishing community are mourning the loss of longtime tournament director, mentor and friend Bill Taylor, who passed away Friday at the age of 79 following a brief battle with liver cancer.
For more than three decades, Bill was one of the most familiar and respected figures in tournament bass fishing. From the early days of Operation Bass through the growth of FLW and eventually MLF, he helped shape how tournaments were operated and how generations of anglers experienced the sport.

reports.title: Ark Gravity AVID BFS Reel Review: A Serious BFS Performer Without the Premium Price
reports.text:
I’ve spent a lot of time fishing bait finesse system (BFS) gear over the past several years, and one of the things I’ve learned is that a good BFS reel needs to do more than simply cast lightweight lures. reports.text:

reports.title: Researchers Sank 140 Trees in a Lake, and Fish Production Doubled
reports.text:
To get more fish in a lake, just add some trees.
That’s the somewhat simplified conclusion of researchers who added 140 “fish sticks” — fallen or cut-down trees — to northern Wisconsin’s 92-acre Sanford Lake. The goal was to see if additional trees either attract fish already in the lake or lead to more of them.
“ In our project, we found that adding trees doubled the number of fish that Sanford Lake can now support,” says Greg Sass, head of the Wisconsin DNR research team.
In other words, add more trees and higher numbers of fish will eventually follow.

reports.title: Yeopim Creek Fliers with Carolina ALL OUT
reports.text:
Fliers are among the most unique panfish in the Carolinas
T he Carolinas are full of numerous species of panfish, and for their size, they all fight like champs. They’re also very tasty. Fliers, although they are found throughout the southeast, are among the least widely distributed panfish, mostly living in swampy, acidic blackwater creeks with low pH.
Where you’ll find fliers, you can always count on finding other panfish as well. They overlap with crappie, bluegill, redbreast and shellcrackers, among other species.

reports.title: How To: Hot Summertime Tactics for catching crappie
reports.text:
Hot Summertime Tactics for Catching Crappie
When summer water gets hot, crappie usually leave the shallow cover and seek cooler, more oxygenated water, shade, and baitfish. The key is finding where those conditions overlap.
Fish deeper: Start around 15–30 feet, then adjust based on your lake’s depth and thermocline. Electronics are extremely helpful for locating suspended schools.
Target brush piles: Deep brush, submerged trees, and man-made structure can hold crappie throughout summer. Slowly work a jig vertically around the cover.
Follow the bait: Find schools of shad or other forage and look nearby—and often directly beneath them—for crappie.
